blocks.text: I said “Not at all!”

“And most remarkable men!” said Mr. Badger confidently. “Captain Swosser of the Royal Navy was Mrs. Badger's first husband. He was a very great and respected officer indeed. Professor Dingo, her husband just before me, is famous across Europe.”
Mrs. Badger overheard him, and smiled.

“Yes, my dear!” Mr. Badger said in answer to her smile. “I was telling Mr. Jarndyce and Miss Summerson about your two former husbands. Both were very great and respected men. They found it difficult to believe, as people generally do.”

“I was only just twenty,” said Mrs. Badger, “when I married Captain Swosser of the Royal Navy. I was in the Mediterranean with him. I am quite a Sailor. Exactly twelve years after our wedding-day, I became the wife of Professor Dingo.”
(“Famous across Europe,” added Mr. Badger quietly.)
“And when Mr. Badger and I married,” Mrs. Badger continued, “we chose the same day of the year. I had grown fond of that day.”

“So Mrs. Badger has had three husbands. Two of them were very great and respected men,” said Mr. Badger, bringing the facts together. “And each time she married on the twenty-first of March, at Eleven in the morning!”
We all said how impressed we were.
“If Mr. Badger were not so modest,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I would politely correct him. I would say three great and respected men.”
“Thank you, Mr. Jarndyce! That is what I always tell him!” said Mrs. Badger.

“And, my dear,” said Mr. Badger, “what do I always tell you? I am not pretending that any success I may have had in my profession is worth little. Our friend Mr. Carstone will have many chances to judge that success. But I am not so foolish—no, really,” said Mr. Badger to us all, “so unreasonable—as to think I am as great and respected as Captain Swosser and Professor Dingo. They were men of the very highest quality. Perhaps this portrait of Captain Swosser will interest you, Mr. Jarndyce,” continued Mr. Bayham Badger. He led the way into the next drawing-room. “It was painted when he returned home from the African Station. He had suffered from the fever of that country while he was there. Mrs. Badger thinks it is too yellow. But it's a very fine head. A very fine head!”
We all echoed “A very fine head!”

“When I look at it,” said Mr. Badger, “I feel, ‘that's a man I should like to have seen!’ It shows very clearly what an outstanding man Captain Swosser was. On the other side is Professor Dingo. I knew him well. I cared for him as his doctor during his last illness. The portrait looks so like him that he almost seems able to speak! Over the piano is Mrs. Bayham Badger when she was Mrs. Swosser. Over the sofa is Mrs. Bayham Badger when she was Mrs. Dingo. As for Mrs. Bayham Badger as she is now, I have the original herself, and no copy.”

Someone now announced that dinner was ready, and we went downstairs. It was a very elegant meal, served beautifully. But Mr. Badger was still thinking about the Captain and the Professor. Ada and I had the honour of receiving his special attention. So we heard all about them.
“Water, Miss Summerson? Let me help you! Please, not in that drinking glass. Bring me the Professor's cup with a stem, James!”
Ada very much admired some flowers made to look real, under a glass cover.
“Amazing how well they last!” said Mr. Badger. “They were given to Mrs. Bayham Badger when she was in the Mediterranean.”
He invited Mr. Jarndyce to have a glass of claret, a red wine.

“Not that claret!” he said. “Excuse me! This is a special occasion. On a special occasion, I bring out some very special claret that I happen to have. (James, Captain Swosser's wine!) Mr. Jarndyce, the Captain brought this wine into the country. We will not say how many years ago. You will find it very unusual. My dear, I shall be happy to drink some of this wine with you. (Captain Swosser's claret for your mistress, James!) My love, to your health!”
